previous.subtitle: Puzzle · Unity
previous.summary: A puzzle game where the player moves a ball by tilting the environment. Each stage introduces a mechanic through a unique space — collect tokens, learn jump and attack, and reach the exit.

highlights.item: Teach-by-space design: no heavy tutorial walls
Core loop: tilt, jump, attack, collect, exit
Three playable levels focused on progressive mastery

intro.paragraph: Level is a puzzle game. The player acts on the environment to move a ball, collect tokens, and advance through three different levels.
The player can use three skills: move, jump, and attack. Victory means collecting tokens and/or defeating enemies, then reaching the exit. Failure is losing all HP or falling off the ground.
The first level teaches movement. The second teaches jump. The third introduces health and attack with a small mini-boss. Mechanics stay simple so level design can carry the experience.

sections.title: History
sections.quote: The utilisation of computers is not intuitive to humans. We must learn how to use it. — Sjoerd “Hourence” de Jong

paragraphs.paragraph: The project began after studying level design through games and books. A line from “The How’s and Why’s of Level Design” stuck: tools are not intuitive — people must learn them.
That raised a question: could a game be intuitive enough that someone plays it naturally without frustration — the way Mario Bros. often feels?
That question became the beginning of Level.
Two precepts guided the work: stay simple enough that players can learn without being taught every mechanic, and force players to use every mechanic that is introduced.
The core mechanic: move the ball by tilting the ground so it travels through the world.

sections.title: Early stage — prototypes
sections.imageAlt: Early Level prototype — ball in free fall

paragraphs.paragraph: Unity physics was unfamiliar territory after mostly 2D tutorial work. The goal was a ball that feels recoverable after mistakes — small initial acceleration, later terminal velocity.
The first prototype was a free-falling ball used to feel velocity and collisions. Targets like “magnitude 4 from rest on a 10° plane within 5 seconds” became reference feel, then adjusted by play.
Wall collisions needed custom bounce logic (reverse pre-impact velocity with AddForce, then correct angles with vector math) before the ground and walls felt natural enough to build levels.

Because Update runs every frame, vertical displacement from Quaternion.Slerp depends on plane size. If per-frame motion stays smaller than the ball collider, the ball follows. If the plane is too large, displacement exceeds the collider and the ball falls through.
Fast left/right tilting near edges makes it worse. Jumping near an edge can reset the plane to identity while the player still holds tilt.
The fix: limit plane length and max rotation, and raise physics refresh rate — which is why long paths in Level 0-2 are successions of small planes instead of one long slab.

sections.title: Mid stage — teaching in the world

paragraphs.paragraph: With mechanics in place, the next goal was forcing players to use them without a separate tutorial. World panels say “exit” or “jump.” Controls stay familiar: WASD/arrows and space.
Rotating tokens with sound invite curiosity; UI confirms collection. Exit animation and ground color cue which platforms can move.
Level 1 teaches tokens, exit, and changing planes. Level 2 teaches jump and falling. Level 3 introduces health and attack.
Playtests with gamers and non-gamers showed the design was not as intuitive as hoped — almost nobody finished without help. Gamers usually learned faster.

Common stuck points: not realizing velocity carries when leaving a tilted plane (~70% of testers), and jumping without building speed first. Non-gamers often repeated the same failing action; gamers tried new options.
The takeaway: exploration habits from games help, but tools still need to be taught before players can invent solutions.
Level was meant to keep game design simple so level design could own difficulty, surprise, and fun — introducing mechanics only after earlier ones felt earned.
The foundation is complete enough to grow: new puzzles, enemies, and maybe a story. Thank you for playing.

previous.lead: Alexandre Guichet is a Python and C++ software engineer with 6.5+ years of experience, based in Vancouver.

body.paragraph: Industry experience in Python, C++, C#, and deep learning / machine learning — plus cloud and big data analysis, data mining with Hadoop, SQL, and Spark. He builds scalable algorithms, ships OOP applications with solid unit testing, and works closely with teams across labs and product orgs.

As Technical Lead at Microsoft he develops ARM silicon firmware (SystemC, C, C++), automates FPGA and silicon validation in Python and C++, and leads automation / SoC validation across four projects — including Azure DevOps standardization and a team of four. Earlier roles include Intel (PCIe / CXL modelling), Evenant and Algolys (full stack), and Bosch (sensor testing and ML for MEMS).
Applied Science at The University of British Columbia (2015–2018). Side craft still shows on this site: Unity games like Level and The Arena, open-source ML work (MFS), and music written for games.

previous.summary: A Real-Time Strategy / RPG hybrid in Unity. The player controls two characters at once in real-time battles, clears tutorial arenas, then explores a dungeon floor.

intro.paragraph: The Arena plays like a Real-Time Strategy / RPG hybrid. The player controls two characters at once in real-time battles and must clear all battles to advance through the story and levels.

Four skills plus auto-attack drive both puzzles and combat. Victory means clearing battles and reaching the end of the first floor; failure is when both characters die at once. The build includes a tutorial arena series and a dungeon floor with world / NPC interaction outside the arena.

sections.title: Level design
sections.imageAlt: The Arena gameplay — dual characters in combat

paragraphs.paragraph: Floors are designed as distinct mechanical chapters rather than copies of the same combat loop.
Spaces ask players to read the arena, switch characters, and sequence abilities — puzzles and fights share the same dual-character grammar.
Two characters means two toolkits. Progress comes from combination, not from a single overpowered kit.
This write-up is carried forward from the original portfolio and will expand as the project continues.

previous.title: Mutual Information Feature Selection
previous.subtitle: Open source · ML · Matlab / Python
previous.summary: A fast, out-of-the-box feature selection algorithm using mutual information for discrete–continuous datasets — with tunable precision vs speed.

highlights.item: Returns decision matrix and selected features

intro.paragraph: Mutual Information Feature Selection (Apr 2020 – Jul 2020) is a fast, efficient open-source feature selection algorithm using mutual information.

It targets discrete–continuous datasets. Pick a dataset, choose how many top features to keep, and the algorithm returns a decision matrix, selected features, and the knobs needed to trade precision for speed.

paragraphs.paragraph: B.C. Ross, “Mutual Information between Discrete and Continuous Data Sets”. PLoS ONE 9(2), 2014.
A. Kraskov, H. Stögbauer, and P. Grassberger, “Estimating Mutual Information”. Phys. Rev. E 69, 2003.
W. Gao, S. Kannan, S. Oh, P. Viswanath, “Estimating Mutual Information for discrete-continuous mixtures”. arXiv:1709.06212, 2017.
